blocks.x: This is Bill Russell speaking at 732 St. Peter Street. We're going to interview Chester Zardas this morning. Can you give your full name? Do you have a middle name?
My name is Chester Zardas and born in 1900. What was the exact date? It's May the 27th, 1900. May the 27th.
I was going to ask a little bit more about this picture. You say it was in Covington around 1921.

Right around that time. How old were you then about, you don't look very old then. No I was a kid then. I was real. I don't think I was 20 years old and that's what I was telling you about. But Buddy was older than me. Yeah. Yeah. Buddy was way older than me. And first of all, well Fissel and Buddy Mann I think they were about the oldest one in the bunch.
Buddy Mann today looks a little older than me.
Yeah he was older than anybody see. And George was older than me. George Washington.
Do you know anything about him, where he came from or what part of town or who he played with? Who else? I know he played with Buddy for Tebitt. I wonder who else.

No I don't know who else George played with. I think George worked a while with Louis Dumaine. Oh yeah. You remember Louis Dumaine? Yeah I'm sure I knew him fairly well. Yeah. Well he worked with Louis Dumaine. And there's another trumpet player a little bit,
Raleigh. Oh let's see. Amos Raleigh. He worked with Amos a long time. You remember Amos Raleigh? Yeah. I didn't know him but his son is still playing.

Yeah. Yeah. Well that's who he worked with. I never knew him. Well he was a pretty good trumpet player at that time. You know what I mean? Yeah. And George Washington worked with him. Yeah. George used to work with him.
Do you know when he died or what happened to him?

Well George was taken sick. George was living at, I remember when he died, he was up at Foice and Ramport. Yeah up in that section. That's where he died from because he was living up there. I used to go to his house, see? Yeah. He had a room up there and I used to go up there. Well that time I drank to the little booze you know. Yeah. And he used to like it so I'd mostly go up there and just past the time away when we wouldn't be working you know because I had my accord in and we'd just go out there and get a couple of bottles of beer and some forth like that. And all of you fellas lived over on this
side then. Or did you move over there when you played there? Well I tell you when we was working

over there we stayed there. You stayed over there then? Yeah. We all lived there together. We stayed there for about four years, four or five years we stayed over there. Over there in Covington or Mansfield? Yeah in Covington. You see because Covington was our headquarters. See because we leave out Covington, we go play in Burgalusa, Picayune, Lumberton. Well we had all that work out there, Harrisburg, and different places you know. Well all that work come from there you see. And that's why we had to stay over there rather than the kids stay over here. And then we was working at the hotel over there, the White Hotel. See we always work at that hotel. What's the name of that hotel? Is it still there? Yeah it's there.
I guess we've heard of it anyway. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Any more about Buddy Manda today? Can you tell us? He played banjo. Did he play guitar too? Well I don't know. I never

seen him play no guitar but he was a good banjo player. Buddy made this banjo there. That's the banjo he made himself. You know what I mean? Yeah it's got an unusual head on it. Yeah, head on it. That's right. It's like a guitar head. And that was a good one too. He made it and he was waiting. Every time he'd catch him he was doing something on that banjo. But he was really good at it.
And can you tell us any more about Buddy Patti since he's not here anymore? I never did get to hear him.

What did he sound like? I know it's hard to explain. Buddy was a nice fella. He was an easy going fella. But he had nice ways, you know what I mean, until he'd get that booze. And he used to like to drink plenty. You know what I mean? He was a man that would drink and would take two tree jobs at one time. Well George Lewis told me that once. Well that's the facts you see. And that's what the ruination of the band. But the people used to like him. Buddy did some things there. I think if somebody else would do that now I think somebody would kill him. You know what I mean? But they just liked him. He was just lucky. And I see one night we played up in Burgalusi and after we played up there the mayor or the sheriff, somebody, didn't pay us the money that night because he told us that they didn't make no money. He said, but you come around tomorrow I'm going to pay you all the more or I'm going to drive down to Covington and pay you money. Buddy got, but he said all right at the first time you know. He pulled around there and started drinking that old corn liquor made last night. That was in probation then. Yeah that was. And Buddy got full of that liquor there. He said come on, drive me to the man. He studied a lot.
Did he stutter all the time? All the time studied. Yes he studied.

Maybe somebody told me. Yes he did. He studied all the time. He said I want you to bring me to the man's house. I want some money. All right. He gets on there and said come on we're going to the man's house. I said we got him in the car and went on down to the man's house. I mean he went to the man's and knocked at the door. Man said who was that? Buddy Petit. So man said what you want buddy? I want some money. So that's where the man said I told you I didn't have no money buddy. Yeah. So he came down and he started talking. He was a nice fellow through the man. So he told the sheriff. He said, oh buddy I told you I don't have no money here. He said now wait until the moron I'll give you some money. He said I'll have some money right now. So the sheriff said wait let me see if my wife got any money. That man had to go back there. He just had $20. He said that's all my wife got $20. He said I'm going to give you this $20. And tomorrow he said don't come here. I'm going to come down to the covenant and bring the rest of that money you know. So sure enough man in the morning the man around 10 11 o'clock he came down there and he told Buddy. He said, Buddy I didn't talk to you to come to my house and wake me up for a few niggas like that. Buddy said I need my money. They said yeah Buddy. He said all them boys need their money too just like you needed but you should have you know should have waited until like I told you and then you would have got the money. So he asked us did we get our money Buddy paid? I said yeah he paid us. Well that's one thing about Buddy. He you know he pay you money. You know what I mean? If he gets you on the job like he said well the job paid so much so much you know. And enough he don't have it if he doesn't spend the money he's going to say well I didn't spend the money and I'm going to have to owe you. Is it all right? Well quite nicely he spent it. You didn't pledge you didn't know that. But it's got to be all right. You know what I mean? So but finally he's a pretty good fella. Buddy was all right.
Where did he live when he lived over here in the city?

Buddy. Buddy was living at 17 something St. Anthony Street. St. Anthony. That's on St. Anthony between the. Yeah, Clayburn and all up in there. Yeah between Durban and that next street room and a little bit of a little house that's back in the yard there.
His name really wasn't Petit. He was raised by old Joe Petit. I knew him.
That's right. You remember Joe? He played trombone.
Yeah. I once made a record of him even. I knew him fairly well. Yeah well that's true. But he never did tell me much about Buddy. Did they adopt him or was he a

stepchild or what? Do you know? I don't know. From the way I think Buddy's mama made friends with Joe, old man Joe see. And Buddy was a small kid at that time from what you know the way I'm figured out. Yeah. And Buddy went on Petit's name started going on his own name. You know what I mean? Yeah. Do you remember what his own name had been? No. I don't know what his own name is.
I can't remember. I think maybe George Lewis told me once it was Crawford. I'm not sure.

I think so. I think you're right. I think you're right. I think that's it. I think George, yeah. I think so. Crawford maybe. I'm not sure though. Yeah. But did he live up in that section most of the time?
I guess that... Who that Buddy? Yeah. I know the old man Joe Petit lived across from Artesian Hall there when I knew him on Durbanon. Durbanon Street, yeah.

Yeah. Near St. Bernard. Yeah. Well he stayed there but most of the time he moved back on Zyga Street back of there, on Zyga and Miro. Back in there? That's where he died back there. Buddy didn't. No, the old man Petit, yeah. Joe Petit. Joe. And one time we had a trombone, just making them buck you know, right at the house there. You remember Ambrose? No, I don't think so. Well that's another trombone player, Ambrose. No, really not. Yeah, but I didn't know his name but he was pretty good in his time. Well that's one of them what you call a tailgate man you know. But he was pretty nice and we'd get him in there to get him two trombones and maybe the whole band would be up there just having fun. You know, a little hustling and different things. Who did he play with most of the time?
Who did Ambrose? Yeah, do you remember?

Yeah, Ambrose was playing with the same little band I will tell you about, the Merritt Band. Well he was playing with that band. There was no name band but I mean it was doing good for the time around here. But there was no band that sells you know. So that's who he was playing with all that

time. I want to ask some more about Buddy Petit. I hope I don't make a news of his own. Oh no, no, no, no. But I never got to hear him. What kind of a tone did he have or what kind of a style? Did he play high notes, low notes most of the time? No, Buddy never did play no high notes.

Buddy was no high notes player. But what Buddy would put down there and in the staff, you're going to enjoy. Did he play a lot of notes? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. Buddy had a whole lot of stuff, a whole lot of stuff but low. I mean he can go low and play more than when he can't high notes. He couldn't play no high notes and he's neck, you know what I mean? He used to come out right there. And Louis Armstrong does that too. Several people do. Yeah. And well I mean Louis come out on one side but Buddy's used to come out on the both sides. And Buddy always had a white lip you know, around there like that.
How was his teeth? In good shape? Yeah, he had nice teeth. Yeah. And Buddy was a nice looking boy. He was nice looking.
You can see on that book there. Oh yes.
He wasn't very large then.
No he never was. He never was. He's very small here.
Yeah, he always was small. But he was a terrible fellow though. Did he always use a coronet? This looks like sort of a sharp coronet.
Yeah, that same trumpet there, a cornet what you called it at that time. Yeah, that's right.
Did he play pretty loud or soft most of the time?
Well he played pretty loud sometimes, yeah. You know what I mean? Catch him in a good humor like he's been out. But then what he used to like, he had a derby you know. Oh yeah.
He used a derby.

Make all that, oh man. Oh Buddy, boy that boy's been something. Did he use mutes much? Yeah, he used a mute, not too much a mute. But he'd take that derby and use that derby a whole lot though. Well after he started using that derby, that's what made that derby famous around here. You take Chris Kelly and Rene. Well after Buddy died, well all them trumpet players start taking that derby. Even Hubert Moran, he started on that style. You know what I mean? He started making the note. Well they made it so that was it.
How did Buddy compare say with Kid Rene? I mean were there styles anything the same or different?

No, there was a different style. Different style altogether. Well both of them boys was tough. They were two good men. But Rene, he was a high man. Yeah, he played high notes. And Rene played something like this boy, Yvonne Thomas. You ever heard of Yvonne Thomas?
Well I've heard about him. Bunk used to talk about him.
Yeah well that's a tough man too. That's a tough man.
In Crowley and New Iberia and all that section.

And you take Bunk, I mean that Bunk, this boy Yvonne, and we used to have a tenor player called Baker. You know? You ever met Baker? No, never met Baker. That's two men. Well I mean we used to work together. I mean duets, you know what I mean? Both of them up there high, trumpet high and that clarinet right under there, playing the same thing. Ours was pretty.
Well how did Buddy compare with Louis Armstrong would you say?

Well Louis, he wasn't the man Louis. I mean Buddy wasn't the man Louis, you know what I mean? But all of them respected Buddy. All of them, because Buddy could play. Buddy used to play. Like I tell you before, he never played those high notes. Yeah I know everybody's told me he was wonderful. But what he played in that staff and down below that staff make you swim in the head. Oh yeah, so much stuff. And then he had a nice springboard. Oh yeah, he had a nice springboard.
I appreciate you telling us about him. I'm going to ask you about yourself here a little bit. I noticed you were using a bow. Yes, I used to use the bow.

Did you use it most of the time? No, on the bows we used to just have occasionally like, you know what I mean? It wasn't regular because the bow didn't go with that jazz music unless you got a soft number. Like a waltz or shardis. Well that's when you use that bow. I was telling that bow every day I got to buy me a bow. I don't have no bow. And that's the only time I used the bow. And I used to take the butt end of this bow and I used to pick that fiddle. Oh with that little knot there. Yeah that frog. I picked the devil out of that fiddle. Because you picked right under the string. Oh yeah, I made a nice name. I used to put that bow. Until after I come in to bring some of the strings and I say I can't buy no string like that and I just
put it down. That was the regular three-quarter size bass. That's three-quarter. Did you always hold your hand out in this position? No, I never hold my hand in that position, no.
I just do that on that picture like that. But I never did hold. See them time, them people didn't care about it. You know what I mean? Yeah, the flap like that. That's right.

That's correct. Yeah. Had all of you been together most of this time? All the time. That's the whole bunch right there. That's the whole bunch. You didn't have any changes back and forth from one to the other.
No, no. That's the whole bunch right there. Because we liked it one another and we liked what we was doing. We just had to start playing together and we liked it.
Can you remember what type of pieces you played? Did you play like for instance many blues or the

late popular songs? No, no. What did you play? It wasn't like that. We played the blues all right. And some of them late ones come out there but say like them old time, It's A Plenty, you know what I mean? Yeah. Well Tiger Rag, we didn't play Tiger Rag much but when the people come ask for it we'd play it. Because this guy here used to like to make that Tiger, you know what I mean? So we'd play it out there unless somebody come and ask for Tiger Rag, we played the Tiger Rag. And did you play mostly for
white dances over there at the hotel or not? Yeah, mostly white dances. Not many colored dances over

there on that side. No, no. We didn't have too many, but we played for them though. He did play some of them. Yeah, because they had a place out in Covenant they called it Romeo Park. See they had a dance hall. You heard about the Romeo? No, I don't know about that. Well they had a park there where the boys used to play ball and we used to play for the ball games and sometimes we'd give the dance right after the ball game like that while we'd play the dance for them like that.
I was wondering, oh excuse me, the band I heard you in the night before last was George Lewis which had done Preservation Hall. How did that sound compared to this band? Was there

much difference in the music faster, slower? Yeah, lots of difference because the music wasn't that fast so like we played over there, you know what I mean? And you take the trumpet like I told you before, there's no man can fit in there like that boy there. You see what I'm talking about? Nelson's a good man on that but these boys was together. You understand? They'd been working together God knows how long. And this band was just put together. Of course the other night you had a piano too, and there's no piano. Did you miss the piano in those days? No, no, we didn't worry about no piano. No we didn't want no piano. We're glad we didn't have no piano because we had too much music coming out there to have a piano because we weren't going to get the right kind of piano maybe,

you know what I mean? There's somebody that'd mess up. Might be out of tune in all the things. Yeah, so we just used like that. We'd take that there and go anywhere. Satisfy anybody. Yeah, them same six pieces you see there. I wonder about your part. Did you play mostly two beat or four beats? Well it was mostly four beats. In those days too. In those days you didn't change your style much.

No, no, no, from today. You see that's what I was talking about, I was telling that boy this morning. The old and time, you see you take the bass, we see loud setters I guess, instruments you know, they play in the bass. They make those kind of different things, you know, for an instant like you play a bass fiddle. You take a young guy today, he sits on in the band, he will make a solo off beat. That's no Dixieland. That's no Dixieland. You see? If you take a man playing Dixieland on a fiddle, he's going to run you some chords, you see? He's going to run all them chords. And you can tell, you know what I mean? You can tell. And that time is just like when you started off with it. But if a man is going to take a solo, well he's off time there. That's the time the drummer can't come in there to catch that man where he's coming in there. So I told him, I told the guy this morning the same thing. I said, you guys play nice bass around this, but they're not playing no Dixieland, they're playing this modern jazz.
How did the drummers play in those days?
Well that's four four beats. Yeah, four four beats. Yeah, the four four beats. Yeah, but he's a good drummer there. Facer was a good drummer.
And the banjo, what did he do in those days?
Well I mean he's giving you that beat. Just the four beats. Yeah, that four beats. Everything was hitting. I mean just like a clock, you know what I mean? That time was so perfect.

And the clarinet was similar to the style they used today? Just like the, yeah. Similar to George Lewis? George Lewis, yeah. Of course we still hear Edmund Hall still plays. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Never changed his style much either I guess. I don't know.

Well like I said, these fellas they've all been together, you know what I mean? And you take like this boy Hall. Hall used to be a terrible man. See? And by being together, working together so long, you know, and different things like that.

He's still real good I think. He still plays good I think. Yeah, George plays nice. I mean Edmund Hall. I haven't heard him for three years. You got one of his records, didn't you? Yeah. I was going to ask, did you always use four strings on your bass or sometimes three? Always did use four strings. Have you ever used a three?

Well I'll tell you, I bought a bass with the same bass I tell you about with the old man. Well he had three strings on that bass. Bill and Moran. Yeah, Bill and Moran. Well after that third, that fourth string, I go to make a G, like sometimes I'm playing a soft number and I have my bow and I will make a low G, you know what I mean? Well I couldn't make my low G. Sometimes I have to finger my G down from this F, you see? And if I didn't finger that G I'd have to make that open G. What I mean by making a G open all the time when it don't sound, you know what I mean? This don't sound right. See because you take music now, if you're reading music, like I used to read the whole other music, and you can't play the three string bass with them dots. You know if you're reading you can't do that. I played a little horn too. I played bass horn too. But I was playing that E flat. I played bass horn. Well not so long. I liked the round here. And the same bar there loved me a whole lot. George. And I said well I didn't like it. I didn't like it. I wake up here at what they say, I played Buddy Petite there, up at St. Charles and Pardis. There used to be a Jitney dance. You know the Jitney dance? That's a dying dance. Yeah. I remember the old Fern and Budweiser. Yeah, yeah. Well that's right. Well I waited up there with Buddy playing that Jitney dance a long time, just playing the horn. I used to have a pretty horn. I had blue lights, green lights, and red lights. When one light go on, they don't want to come on, you know. It won't go off. Yeah, I've seen those.
Yeah. That was pretty. Yeah, that was good. I was going to ask you about this band. If you had any pieces that you all composed, or did Buddy ever write any music? Do you know of any songs?

No, Buddy never did worry about no music like that. But he could spell a little bit. Buddy could read a little bit. Yeah, but he never did worry about. Or make up any tunes. I mean even if they weren't written
down, you know if he ever wrote any, or composed any, made them up or anything.

No. No. No. Sometime you take like, he get a number, and if he learned a number, he's going to come tell us, well we've got a new number. We just try it before people come in. We're going to play right there. All right after the banjo, get on in there and him and this boy, and that. Well them three they're going to slow, you know what I mean? Well a little while after that I come on in there and I'm hitting, you know what I mean? After I be hitting like that, well that tramo was going to come in there. So Edmund Hardy said well let's go, so we're going to play this thing a new number, you know what I mean? Well he done learned the number. Well that's really because I couldn't read at that time myself. But George he could read a little bit, and I think Edmund could read, but this man he couldn't read. No, and the drummer couldn't read, you know what I mean? And Buddy could read a little. Yeah, Buddy could read a little, he could spell.

Yeah Buddy could spell. But he was fine boy though. I was going to ask you again about your very early life, which you didn't tell so much about when you were going over that material. You were born 1900 you say? That's right. Can you tell us anything about your parents? Did they play any instrument?

No, I'll tell you what, when I told you before like Billy went to summon that bass for five dollars, I told my mother I was going to buy that bass. Did she sing or play piano? My mama? No. My mother didn't want me to play. No fiddle at all, no kind of music. She said, the musicians was no good. You understand? Because the women runs behind musicians too much. So I wanted to learn to fiddle after this man, Billy Marrera, can play so much fiddle. I said, well I'm going to have to learn. So when I asked him and he said yes, he said I could learn, he said I think you'd make a good musician. Had you ever played anything else before that? I used to hit on the ghetto. Yes I did. Did you pick that up yourself? Yes. Me and my cousin, we used to just play, he used to pick the guitar in that second, you know what I mean, the changes like that.
Who was your cousin? Did he ever work as a musician?
No, no. He just was a fellow that just worked hard for a living, never stood about no music.
Did you have any brothers or sisters that played anything?

Nobody, nobody. I'm the only one in my family. I had a cousin one time, he played the fiddle, he tried to play but at that time you know what I mean, anything do. His name was Gus Green. He was trying to play the bass like that. Well I was going to ask what part of
town you came from, or you were born right in the city here.

I was born right here in the Seven Ward, see that's at St. Bernard and Robertson, between St. Bernard and Annette, the 1600 block, that's 1650 North Robertson. I'll never forget that number. Yeah. That was some good old days. Because at that time we used to play at the market. The market used to be open. The same Bernard market? The same Bernard market, yeah. The same band there. That's what I tell you. Did that band been together? Yeah, the same band.
What were the very first bands you heard, or what music can you remember? Even when you were a little kid five or six years old or something, can you remember hearing any bands or parades,
or what kind of music did you hear of those days? You mean them big bands playing the brass band?
Or anything, or did you ever listen to the dance bands outside when you were a kid, or what did you hear?

Oh yeah, I used to listen to that. Well I tell you, you see when I was born at the Lord like that, I went all around those places just to hear a different band, give me an idea. You know what I mean? Well I heard a lot, but I mean for you talking about what tune they played and so on?
Well I just don't know whose band they were and what the music was like.

Yeah well this same man that learned me I used to be around his band most of the time. Billy Moran. Billy Moran, he had the Olympia band. And this boy I know who used to play, I know Matoya, he was playing with them. And Big Sidney, Sidney Dave was playing Crannert, you know him. Well that's another tough man. And John Moran was playing guitar. He was playing guitar. But he was a tough man. And after, well I'd go around by him all the time, he'd let me sit on in, he'd play, because he'd be learning me. He'd be making something, he'd be like, make that, take that, make it. Well I mean the band still be playing but I'd be going in there and I wasn't good as he was,

but I mean it would give me an idea, you know what I mean? Who were some of the other good bass players? Well he's starting, Bill Moran's son. Simon. You ever heard of Simon? Yeah I've heard of Simon. You got a record of him? No, I don't think he made any, yeah he made some records for Settles to him, but otherwise I never knew him.

Well that's another nice boy. And then he got another brother, played bass too, Eddie. Eddie Moran. Yeah we interviewed him. And Lawrence Moran, you got him too didn't you? Well that's all brothers. So we all came up just as brothers, because we used to go down there and Simon would take the bass, I'd take the bass, and you know what I mean, we'd get together with one another, the show one another. Where did they live in those days? They was living down at Spain Street on Spain between Vire and Oikwar. That's where they were living at that time because sometimes I would go to school and I'd leave my school and go around there because Maronese Street is not far from there, it's about two blocks from where they were staying. And I'd go to school over there. I mean I'd go there alone because, see I was just about finished up almost then because I was in I think it was seventh grade then. And I stayed there until, well I finished eighth grade over there. You mentioned something about a Catholic school, were you raised as a Catholic? No, that's a public school, that was a public school. You weren't raised as a Catholic. Yes I was raised as a Catholic. I'm still a Catholic. I'm still, yeah. You see, I keep there. Yeah, because I made first community right up here at St. Catherine.
Yeah, that's right. A couple of other questions I had. Did you play with Chris Kelly?
Yes, I worked with Chris a long time. Yes, I worked with Chris Kelly a long time. I worked with all them big star trumpet players around here, all of them. All of them, yes sir.
Who was your favorite trumpet player, if you had to pick one to hear again? Today? Yeah. Who would you rather hear?

Well, that's the question though. That's the question. Thanks to all them boys play so much. I mean, you know what I mean? When you get with them boys you just, you know, you just don't know who is who. Yeah, they're all great. Oh yeah, all of them is good. All of them is good. Yeah, them boys was something. Take like Rene, he's good, you know what I mean? Them higher notes. Buddy Petit, he's good with them notes down there and then in the staff. But he puts so much in that staff till you disregard that man with them higher notes because I mean it's hitting so smooth, you know what I mean? And then he's filling in there. Oh yeah. Buddy was a man. Yeah, he's gone, but he'll never be forgotten. No, I wish I could have heard it. I wish so too. I wish so too. Yeah, Buddy was all right. Buddy's fine.
Now what style did Chris play? Can you tell us any more about him?
Well Chris played during, he had a nice style he's on. He always owned his own style because you take, Chris give you a double beat, you know, one up and one down, see? But you take most of the
musicians and give you that. Chris would rock his foot back and forth on the heel and the.

Yeah. That's the way Chris do, see? Now you talk about a hymn man, a man played a hymns, whatever, he was a hymn man. He played most all kinds of hymns, yeah. Somebody told me he played a lot of blues too. Yeah, he liked the funny blues, but he was a hymn man. He played more hymn, you know what I mean? Well that time people didn't like no hymns, there ain't no dance. But he used them in dances. Yeah, he used to like them, yeah. That's so, he liked them plenty. You mentioned he used the, that wah-wah, yeah. That's right. He had the mute and the little thing on the side of that mute and wah-wah all the same. The rubber plunger. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
I was asking more about your early life, the bands you heard, any brass bands, parades much you heard?

Yeah, I heard lots of brass bands. I used to follow the brass bands, such as Tuxedo Brass Band. They had a nice brass band. Yeah, that tuxedo was good. You ever heard of it before? Oh yes, that's the original. Yeah, they were good. And I tell you another band I heard, that Onward brass band.
Do you remember who all was in that?
No, so long I forget them fellas. I know Lois Dumain, he was one, he used to play with those boys.
Somebody told me Manuel Perez was playing with the Onward too. How did he sound?

Manuel? I was a sweet trumpet player. Did you ever play with him? No, I didn't play with, every time that Manuel had wanted me, looked like that same boy that would be all you know. And he'd tell me, he'd say, boy I'd like to get you to play in my band. He'd say, but by the time you turn around you're playing with Buddy. So I told him, I said, well you know how it is when you started up with a bunch. I said, you like to be with them, you know what I mean?
So he said, well yeah you're right.

He said, well I never did play with Manuel. But Manuel was a man though. He was a man. Now this Manuel I was telling you about Billy, Manuel was playing with Billy a long time. You see? Because Billy was the manager of the band. See in them times they'd take them fellas, they used to wear them caps, I don't know if you remember.
I've seen pictures of them.

Captioning them coats, they would tape down the legs, you know what I mean? There was one with the Superior band, the same place where Billy was manager of that I think. Yeah, yeah. Well he was manager of that same band, the Erika band. That's the Erika. That's the other band I was telling you about. Onward? The Onward band, yeah.
Can you tell me about any other bass players at that time that you heard, string bass? String bass? Yeah. Who were the best players in addition to Billy?

Well I'll tell you who was good, you take this old boy, I forget his name. He died a good while back. But Johnny was a good boy. Johnny played a whole lot of bass. Johnny what was his name? Johnny Lindsey. Oh Johnny Lindsey, yeah. And you take Pop Foster, he was in that one. He was around there, them fellas been playing way before me, but after I started while we were all, you know, they recognized me, you know what I mean? And they had another old boy who used to be up there with Coochie Morton, do you remember
Coochie Morton? No, but I know about them, but Kit Aurier told me about those. Yeah, the Mortons, yeah.
The Martin Brothers. Yeah, the Martin Brothers, yeah.
They played guitar I guess. Yeah.
And drum, some of them did drums. Yeah, Hendry, Hendry's playing with them, Hendry Morton. Well they had a guy who used to play with them around there, I forget that guy's name.

Oh look here, this is the old Peerless band. Do you recognize the guitar player there? That's Henry Kimball, and that's Bab Frank and McCurdy. And this guitar player, do you know? No, I don't know me. They have him down there as Coochie Morton there. Oh, oh yeah, I know Coochie. Does that look like him?
No, that don't look like Coochie. Coochie done changed so much the last time I yelled, I saw Coochie, you know. No, I see that, Coochie Morton. Yeah. But he was a good man though, he was a good man.
Did you hear Kimball, Henry Kimball, the old man?

The old man, yes. The old man was good. He was good. That's who I wanted to call his non, I forgot his name. Old man Kimball. That's right. Well him and I, we, I used to go to his house too, and him and I used to, you know, used to run over to fiddle, gather like that, and he used to show me a whole lot of stuff on the fiddle, you know. The same old man Kimball. He was living up at Annunciation and Geraintil at that time. That's where he died, up there. Yeah, old Kimball was all right.
See somebody told me once about Jimmy Brown and they played with Manuel Perez sometime on bass. Do you remember Jimmy Brown?

I don't remember Jimmy Brown. It must have been before my time. Yeah. I didn't know Jimmy Brown. And then this old man used to play, of course he didn't play no whole lot of bass, but I mean he used to play, well me give him ideas, what's his name, Albert Glennie? Oh yes.
Old man Glennie?

I forgot about him too. Yeah. Old man Glennie. He lived over in your neighborhood there too. Yeah. And I'll tell you another boy used to play some nice bass, Cleo. You hear the author of Cleo? I've heard of him but never knew him. Well he got killed after hearing the go. He was waking on the ship.
George Geno I remember told me about him.
Yeah, yeah. So he was a pretty nice little bass player.
Most of the fellas play on the four string bass in the time you knew, or many of them used three strings. Glennie used three for a while.

Well I mean no, they all wasn't using four strings, they always using three string bass. You see most of the time you take like, you know time goes by and if a guy see you with four strings, you know, give a dog up, he goes, don't use that string, he'll put it on there anyhow, you know what I mean? Because he doesn't know what it's for. So them guys would get that string and put that string on there. But I mean like I said, if you're reading music and you get used to it, you can't play a fiddle, reading music with three strings. It's not going to sound, that G is not going to give you a good tone. How did they tune them?
What notes did they tune them to? Just the upper three strings or did they change and differ? No, just the upper, just like this. In four notes apart, not in fifths. That's right.
No, no, no, no, no, no. You're talking about like ukulele, it's like. No, no, no, straight, just straight. E, A, D, G. Yeah, straight.
I was going to ask about your very first band that you played in, your very first job. Do you remember the first time you ever got paid for playing, let's say?

Yeah, I remember the first time I got paid. I played with these boys here. No, not these boys, the Merit band, M-E-R-I-T. Yeah, I don't know them. Well you don't know them. Well that's the first band I played with. We played a little party on very, between Seminole, right back in my house, between Seminole and Nannick. All right, well, first time, me, Green, I didn't know, you know what I mean? We get there and we tune up. We had a fellow by the name of Willie Phillip. You ever heard of him, a trumpet player?
Not sure.

Maybe. Well he was no big man, but he could read pretty much. And we had another fellow who was playing the trombone, but he was playing a vowel trombone, his name was Charlie, we called him Big Charlie, big tall man, we had about, oh man, he was about seven foot tall, eight foot tall. And he had that little bit of trombone, the vowel trombone with the keys, you know, playing like that. And that's the first job I played, so we made, I think it was two dollars.
And how old were you about?

Oh I was about between 19 and 20, something like that. Yeah, just about. Because I was working, and I told my mother I was going to play music tonight, she laughed at me, and people are going to run you out there, go around and make all that noise. I said no, they're not going to run me out there, I said I'm going to work. So sure enough I went, we played that job, and the people treated us nice.
Was it a party or something?

Yeah, it was a house party. That's for the whites, you know. And they treated us so nice, so after we knocked off, we knocked off at twelve o'clock, we made that two dollar, two and a half, I just remember what it was. So when I got home, I told my mom, I said, yeah, mom. So I gave her the two dollars. I said, you see, you say they're going to throw me out. I said, they didn't throw me out. I said, they gave me two dollars. I said, that's two dollars. So she said, well that's mighty nice. It's like that. So all right, so that next Saturday we played another job down on Frenchman Street, Frenchman in Ramport. We used to have a dance hall upstairs there. So we played that dance. And this boy, Vincent, I forget his other name, but he was running the dance down there. So we did good, we signed all right. So they gave us another job for that following Saturday.
Who was the trumpet for that? Will Phillip. That same Will Phillip.

Yeah. So we did pretty nice. And all the while, and that's where Buddy come along then. Buddy would talk with me, you know, Buddy Manity. Buddy said, hey there. I said, I heard about you. I said, yeah, Mr. Buddy. I said, I'm doing pretty good. He said, how about you coming over with us? I said, well that'd be all right. I said, all right, so that's where I'll play that next job with them boys that Saturday. And I told them that I was going to go with Buddy Petit. All right, Buddy started getting jobs then at the St. Bernard Market. Buddy Petit was already with Buddy Man today. Yeah. Yeah. Them two been together before we did. And after that so we got the job at the market. Playing this for the opening tomorrow, you know, the people would come and buy stuff. And we played man for about two or three Saturdays. Well the job was paying more. I think we got three and a half or something. And we did all right. So after that so we decided after we played at that hotel, I can't think of that hotel. I think it was Centannomy Hotel up here. Might be. Yeah. Centannomy Hotel.
Centannomy Parish.

Well we used to work there. We worked there for a long time. And they had some old boys used to be around and they liked to follow us, some white boys, you know. And that group used to get together and give dances over there all the time. These keep us busy. And they used to keep us going, we used to go to Ponchatoula. They used to take us from Covenant and go to Ponchatoula.
How did you all travel in those days?
Well we had an old car. We used to double up in there. Old Ford car. That's what we used to travel in.
And when you'd go back and forth on the lake, did you take the boat usually? Or?
You mean when we'd go to the lake from here?
Across the lake, like the Covenant, of course you lived over there too.

We lived it over there, yeah. But you see we used to go across on the boat, that camellia, they had a camellia boat what I was telling you about, you see. And that's the time which then people would pay our way on the boat, you see, to come home and go back. You know what I mean? And now's the time the man, the captain of the boat, he wouldn't take our money to come on that boat. He just let us ride because we had a big name over there and he used to come to the dances where we used to play all the time. And what made him did that because one time we came across on that boat and they had a whole lot of people on there. So he came to Buddy and said, hey Buddy, how about you all knocking a little piece there, man, wake it up on this boat. So he said, all right, all right, we'll do that. So man, we took out our instrument, man, we started playing on that boat there and the war, on the war that music sounds good, you know. And boy, them people, man, they come there and they start putting money in our hat. They took one of our hats, you know, put it down there. And man, we start putting money in there. So that's where after we finished playing, the captain said, play one more, buddy, one more. That's all, that's all. We played one more. So all them people, every time we play a number you get that, you know. I said to myself, well I'll be doggone all this money is flying around in the house. That time money was money. You know what I mean? It's plenty of money now but it don't mean nothing now. You know what I mean? Buy a number. So that's where you all, but what Buddy did, Buddy said, well, we're going to stay on this boat till we get over. I said, okay. But one thing about it, if one man would say something, the rest would agree. You know, I've been in lots of bands, if one man would say something like that, the other guy would tell you, say, well man, we better not do that or I don't want to do it. You know what I mean? One guy is always contrary to the rest. You always got along good the whole bunch together. Yeah. But that band there, I must say myself, everybody was agree. I see we went out one night, just want to have fun, and went out the whole band. There's a guy they call Antwine Griffins, he had a restaurant down the street, you know, from where we live. So we said, we go down there and play down there, wake them up. So we liked it to play. And we went down there, man, and boy, a little while after that, that place was like that, and we started playing. That man took my soul out all the stuff that he had to sell, you know, and soft drinks and all that. Well he gave us two dollars a piece. But I mean that was money, you know what I mean? At that time, sure man. You had fun to do with it I guess, or you wouldn't have gone in the first place. Yeah, but I see the way we did out there, we had our own house out there. You know, we rent a house, and we had it all furnished off and everything like that. And we didn't have no women's at all. We used to do our own cooking even in the house, you know. That's the way we used to live out there. That's why I tell you we stayed out there a long time. Yeah, we did a whole lot of cooking out there, because that's the time my old buddy managed to get the banjo player there. He'd get up there and go out to the store and get lots of stuff and come on, because we all gave him the money, we'd chip in so much, and he'd go out there and get all that stuff and come back there and cook that stuff up there.
And you think that was around 1920 maybe or 21 or something?
That's around 20 or 21. It's around that time between 19 and 21. Yeah. That's all. Well what time, they got 20 on there.
Yeah, Edmund Hall gave him that date. He thought it was about 1920, but I thought maybe he wasn't real sure.
Yeah.
Well it's around that time.
He thought he was trying to check with somebody else.
Yeah. It's around that time. Because once you talked like it might have been a little later, you maybe played with Buddy in the late 20s.

Well I tell you, the way that was, like I told you before, you see I was so much in demand. And they didn't have much fellas to play the bass that after I learned was playing. And this band don't have no job like tonight, or this band got jobs for two, three nights, so maybe, well I'd leave my band, I'd go with that band. You see what I'm talking about? Well this man asked me to join in the band. I said yeah I'll join the band. So I tell this man I can't play them, I'm playing with so and so now. See what I'm talking about? Well all right I'll stay with that band until they don't get no work. Well after they didn't get no work, another band got work and they want me, well I go with that other band. But the way I do that I always keep them in the class all the time. I don't tell them that I want to be with them and be with the other band too. I never did was a man to believe in playing with two bands, you see, because I know I couldn't play with two bands. I had to play with one band, you see. So I was always a straight fellow on that subject, you see. So we got along pretty nice and everything, all the boys, you know, they liked it one or another and what we was doing we liked it. And so that's what makes anybody, I mean anything to take up a few, like what you're doing and you continue on doing it, you know what I mean? You get a kick out of it, that's what I'm talking about. Well that's nice. See right there tonight I played up there? I like that. You see, and I take my bass, I turn my bass, that tone is hitting that wall. See when it hit that tone.
Well I wonder because later you started out facing more of the door and then later you had your bass facing the wall.

That's right, when it hit that wall, that tone's gone, yes Lord. The guy came and asked me, he said, what you got, an amplifier on there? I said no, I don't have no. He said, yeah you got, he said, what makes that bass sound so loud? I said it was just the way I played.
Just the way you played it. As soon as you started out Jaffe came out and said, you really hear the bass tonight?

Yeah. So he looked, he said, man, he said look over there. He said you play as hard. I said I always did, ever since I knew my pitch. I was playing at 8th and Ramport. I was playing at the Bulls Club. Yeah. And you can hear my fiddle from 8th and Ramport to Claiborne and 3rd at the National Park.
You remember the National Park? I've heard about it, yeah.

That's where every time I'd be playing, them guys come up there and say, man, I hear that fiddle way down there. I said, oh good. I said, you're just pulling my leg. He said, no man. He said, really? I hear that fiddle down there. Well all right, if two, three fellas telling you the same thing, you know what I mean? It must be true. Yeah, that's right. I was going with a girl and she lived at Robinson and Thurid. So that night after I knocked off the job I went to her house and she told me, she said, you know, I was up there sitting down looking out the window. You know, I hear that fiddle, this is good. I said, oh you hear somebody else playing. She said, oh no, she said they don't have nothing else on the Monday night. Around here she said, but the Bulls Club. She said that's the only bass she had. So I said, yeah, it must be true then. Because I met a guy who was telling me the same thing, you know what I mean? Yeah, that's strange.
You could hear it that far.
Oh yeah. So I just took it for granted. Sometime I'd be playing at the National Park. And that same old Jack Carey.
I was going to ask you about Jack Carey because we have a picture of Punch playing at National Park once.
With Jack?
I think he was with Jack maybe. I don't know who else was in the band. They got the whole band?

If I can find the picture. Yeah, well okay we can get it after. So Finney's telling you, well Punch was a terrible man with that, but Punch never could play like the rest of them guys, but he was good though. Punch was good. Yeah, Punch was a good man. Yeah, Punch was really good.
Here's the picture with the, no it isn't Jack Carey, it's Eddie Morris and George Boyd on
the past. Yeah, yeah, yeah. That's George Boyd all right. Yeah.
How did Punch play in those days?

Well Punch was a pretty good man. He was a pretty good man, but I mean he wasn't like the rest of them fellas. I mean he plays nice. And he's style of playing. But I mean he didn't have that style like Rosetta Boyd, you know what I mean? Like Rene and those kind of things. Rene and Chris Kelly. Yeah. Now I used to take, when we'd be on advertising, after we started getting them trucks, you take like Rene. Now he'd take old Rene, now he'd get out there, sometime he gets on out there on the ground. Sometime he sat up on top of the cab like that, oh man he sat down and blow. That's what I told somebody, I say the people that they, I say all that good music, they was getting that good music for nothing. I say today they're going and they're paying big money to get all that kind of jitty bug and you know, rock and roll and all that kind of money. I say when the good music, I say the people didn't pay nothing. I say because you take, sometime we have three bands. Two bands right there lined up and the other band right there crossway to keep. The good band he's going to get the crossway now, he doesn't want you to leave. See? It looked like every time it happened I'd be with one of them good bands. And I used to like it, and I'd be back there sitting down there, just as glad and happy you know. But I know we're going to get some fun you know. So we start there, I say all right boy, we play so and so and so. Okay. So the leader he knock it off there man, we start playing that song and down there. And boy after we get finished playing, more the people they all, you can tell what's the best band because the people going to play it, you see? After they apply to the best band we know that was our band, you know what I mean? So we just say well we got it. But we stay there though, we stay there until they all get off. See when they all go, say well let's go. Then we go. Sometimes we, oh man we stay there, we don't have time to make the routes where we're supposed to make you know. But that was good days though. I was going to ask about Sidney Desbeam. Did you ever play with him?
Yeah I worked with Sidney, I worked with Sidney Desbeam.
But I don't know, I didn't care about working with Sidney. Sidney is a peculiar fellow, you know what I mean? Sidney is a fellow, he uh, I don't know, he just something different attitude from the
He died out in California about four or five years ago. Yeah, I heard that.
Yes.
I met him out there and I'd never known him here. I did hear him once in time but never talked to him before. I saw him in California.

Yeah. So he had a boy, used to work with him, bass violin, called Ranson. You might have heard of him. Yes I've heard of him. Ranson. He was doubling, he was playing bass fiddle and the horn. Well most of the time that boy would be at my house every day learning what I was learning him, you know what I mean? And I learned him until he got to be a tough man. And he worked out there on that sand boat where I was working at. He worked there a long time with Sidney Desbeam. And I worked in his place several times on that boat and I worked at the country club in Ranson's place where Sidney Desbeam, you know. And right there at the Pelican, Ramport and Gravia. Yeah. Do you remember when you used to give dance up there?
I've been in there, yeah.
Years ago. Well I worked there a lot of time with Sidney. So like I told you, I played with most of the best bands around this town at that time.
Do you remember when you played with Elmer Talbert? Did you ever work with him?

Yeah I worked with Talbert a long time. I worked with him, yes. He was a pretty nice trumpet player. Talking about, what's his name, Kukie? He lived at Dumaine and Claiborne there, Talbert. What's his other name? Kukie. Kukie. Kukie. Yeah. He's got a son now in California. He's dead two years ago. Yeah, yeah. I heard that he died. But you were in Philadelphia I guess.
A lot of those sons died. Yeah, yeah. How long were you in Philadelphia?
I stayed in Philadelphia from 40, 45 I believe. No, I left for...
You were there in 44 I know, because you made those records with George Lewis when I was
here in 43.

The next year I came down and they said you were in Philadelphia. I didn't even have your address. That's why that money I owed you all those years. I didn't even know where you were except they said you were in Philadelphia.

Well I was living in North Philly. I lived on 12th and Girard. See, I even bought a home over there. I bought a nice home over there. And because I was thinking the time when I left Denver, Colorado, that's when I left George Morrison's band, you know, like I told you. Well I came to Philadelphia after that and I started working with Henry Lowe's band. That's the secretary of the local out there. Well I played with his band and played a nice long time.
I was going to ask about recordings. In the old days they didn't make many records here I guess.
No they didn't make any records. You made those at George Lewis and some with Bunk. Yeah, yeah.
Did you ever make any others?
No, I didn't make any others. No, I did not. Because last time we made those records was on Canal Street, weren't they?
Yeah, the first ones were in Canal Street. And the ones we made was over at the Gypsy Tea Room. Gypsy Tea Room, remember?
Gypsy Tea Room, that's right. That's right. That's correct. That's right. That's correct. But you never get any of those records, I would have changed the name on them records, the label.

I have that one you made with Bunk. We can play it after a while if you have it. Yeah. We'll be through here in about five minutes. Yeah, so. I was going to ask about the rhythm section. What kind of a rhythm section would you rather work with? A guitar or banjo or piano or what? If I had to work? Yeah. And the drummer, I mean how big a section would you rather have? Piano and drums and guitar or banjo, how big a rhythm section?

You know, I'll tell you why. I'd rather work just with the ghetto, if I got a good ghetto player. You see, you're going to take trouble to find a piano player going to work with the ghetto, bass, and the drums. You see, you don't get all piano players to work with, you know, the way you support. You see, it's a different thing. Like, I can't say what I want to say. But anyhow, if you've got a piano player that understands, you'd like some of these, oh guys, like Lang, you know Lang. I can't remember. Lang was playing with George Louis that, a little bright fellow, a red fellow who played the piano so much. I mean George Williams.
No, I don't think I knew him. Anyway, go ahead. So that's where, oh you take, well somebody, you got to be together on those things, you

know what I mean? Because of, well you take a man of, say like some piano players, but you know, these bass don't be with my bass and that drum. You know what I mean? So sometimes you hitting, he's going to hit after beat.
You know what I mean? Getting too fancy, too much stuff in there.

Yeah, he tried some of them, this can't come up to that swing. You see a whole lot, I've been with lots of bands where the piano player couldn't make it. You see? Now if he was a piano player that not to play so loud, and just kind of take it easy and let the bass and the drums and the guitar player be heard, he'd make out better. But if he can try to race and he can't keep up that time and hit an after beat, he's sparring everything. See what I'm talking about? So you take that for guitar or drum. But mostly you find a drummer, he's going to give you some time. Who were your favorite drummers that you liked to work with in all the years you've worked with?
At that time? All the years you can remember. Who were the best drummers?

Well there's a lot of drummers around here I like to work. What I like to do is George Williams was born. You know George Williams? He died just last year. Yeah he died, that's right. And you take this boy, Lionel, the boy was up there that night there. What's his name? That night we played up there. At the hall there?
That was Dave Oxley. Not Dave, I'm talking about the boy coming there.
The one who came in there, he's a drummer.
Oh wait, I can't think. Saeed Fraser.
No, not Saeed.
No.

In the old days who were the best drummers did you think? Well that boy there, that Faso boy was one of the tops. And you take Saeed, Saeed was a good man then too. He used to be a good drummer. And this boy, Burgard, B-Gard, yeah. Well that was another good drummer.
Who were the best guitar players you liked to work with?
The best guitar? Well you take like Joe Moreri, that was one of the stars around here, you know what I mean? And I said the fellas used to-
He played banjo most of those days?

No, he was playing guitar. No, no, no, no. You used more banjo now than they ever did you, to my knowings, you know what I mean? Yeah. But it was nothing but guitar. And then they didn't have no amplifier or no guitar. You liked the guitar better than banjo. Yeah, the guitar better. Yeah, you get more support and you get much of a solid foundation and more of a music out of a guitar than what you do out of a banjo. Oh yeah. Of course that banjo is all right I mean for like around here like that. It's louder and there's more. Yeah, but I mean you don't get nothing too much out of a banjo. Was the guitar loud enough in the old bands that the drummer didn't cover them up, huh? No, no, no. You take most of the guitar players nowadays, they're using amplifiers.
Oh yeah, I don't like those so much myself. How do you like those?

What's that, amplifiers? Yeah. No, I don't like no amplifiers. That's why when that guy asked me the other day, the other night there, he said, you must be God to amplify on that bass and hang on heaven. He said, well why did it be so loud? I said, I don't know. He come there and he looked. He said, well I'll be God to him. He said, I didn't thought that you'd be playing this by your, you know, natural like that or such right. He said, well this is the loudest bass that I ever heard. He said, I heard some basses, you know, guys playing basses. He said, but this is the loudest one I ever heard. He said, I've been around lots of bands. So I said, well thank you anyhow.
You know what I mean? Did you ever play for Johnny St. Cyr?
Yes, that's a good man. I played with Johnny a long time with the bunk, that same bunk. We made some records. Johnny was on that record.
I don't know if he was on that record.
But we made something together. You did? Yeah, Johnny St. Cyr. I heard Johnny got hooded some time ago.
Just like you got. The public's eyes had an accident, but he's all right now. I think that's about, the tape is just about ready to run out.
Well I heard he made a record out there. Yeah, he was in an accident.
He shouldn't drive with his arm. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
